title: Functions: Notation, Composite and Inverse Functions
description: Function notation f(x), solving f(a) = b, domain and range, composite functions fg(x), and inverse functions f⁻¹(x) for IGCSE Maths 0580 Extended.

notes.heading: The Function Machine: f(x) Notation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A function is a rule that turns each input $x$ into exactly one output. The notation $f(x)$ means 'the output of function f when the input is $x$'.

🔑 How it works
To evaluate a function, substitute the input value for $x$ everywhere it appears in the rule, then calculate.

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = 4x - 1$, so $f(3) = 4 \times 3 - 1 = 11$.

💡 Worked Example 2
$g(x) = x^2 + 2$, so $g(4) = 4^2 + 2 = 16 + 2 = 18$. Square first, then add.

⚠️ Common Mistake
$f(3)$ is not $3f$ and does not mean 'f times 3' — the $3$ is an input, not a multiplier.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $f(3)$ is a single number: the output when $x = 3$.
• Each function has its own rule; letters like f, g, h are just names.

✅ Check
If $h(x) = 3x$ then $h(5) = 15$.

notes.heading: Solving f(a) = b
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
To find the input that produces a given output, set the rule equal to the output and solve the resulting equation.

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = 3x$ and $f(a) = 21$. Then $3a = 21$, so $a = 7$.

💡 Worked Example 2
$f(x) = 5x - 3$ and $f(a) = 27$. Then $5a - 3 = 27$, so $5a = 30$ and $a = 6$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing the wrong way: from $5a - 3 = 27$ you must add 3 before dividing, giving $a = 30 \div 5$, not $a = 27 \div 5$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'f of a equals b' is just an equation in disguise — solve it as usual.
• If the rule squares $x$, expect two solutions: $x^2 = 9$ gives $x = 3$ or $x = -3$.

✅ Check
$f(x) = 2x + 1$ with $f(a) = 15$ gives $a = 7$.

notes.heading: Mapping Diagrams: Inputs and Outputs
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A mapping diagram shows inputs connected by arrows to the outputs they produce. Each input has exactly one output, but an output may receive arrows from more than one input.

🔑 How it works
Read the mapping as (input, output) pairs. A function that sends two different inputs to the same output is called many-to-one.

💡 Worked Example 1
The rule 'add 7' maps $2 \mapsto 9$, $5 \mapsto 12$ and $10 \mapsto 17$. Every input has its own output: this is one-to-one.

💡 Worked Example 2
The squaring rule maps both $3 \mapsto 9$ and $-3 \mapsto 9$. Two arrows land on 9, so squaring is many-to-one.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying '9 maps to 3 and also to -3'. The arrows go from inputs to outputs: under squaring, 9 maps to 81. It is the *output* 9 that has two inputs.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One input → exactly one output (that is what makes it a function).
• A many-to-one function has no inverse function unless the domain is restricted.

✅ Check
Under the rule 'multiply by 2', the input 6 maps to the output 12.

notes.heading: Domain and Range
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The domain is the set of inputs the function is allowed to use. The range is the complete set of outputs it produces from that domain.

🔑 How it works
Apply the rule to every value in the domain and collect the results, writing each output once. From a graph, the domain is the set of x-values covered and the range is the set of y-values covered.

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = x^2$ with domain $\{-2, 0, 3\}$ gives range $\{0, 4, 9\}$ — note $-2$ does not appear in the range.

💡 Worked Example 2
$f(x) = x^2 - 2$ on the integer domain $-3 \le x \le 2$. The outputs are $7, 2, -1, -2, -1, 2$, so the range is $\{-2, -1, 2, 7\}$: smallest value $-2$ at $x = 0$, largest value $7$ at $x = -3$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
For squaring rules, the largest output does not have to come from the largest x — $(-3)^2 - 2 = 7$ beats $2^2 - 2 = 2$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Domain: inputs. Range: outputs.
• List each range value only once, even if two inputs share an output.

✅ Check
$f(x) = x^2$ on the domain $\{1, 2\}$ has range $\{1, 4\}$.

notes.heading: Composite Functions: fg(x)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A composite function applies two functions one after the other. $fg(x)$ means $f(g(x))$: do $g$ first, then feed its output into $f$.

🔑 How it works
Work from the inside out. Evaluate the inner function first, then substitute its result into the outer function.

$$fg(x) = f(g(x)) \quad \text{but} \quad gf(x) = g(f(x))$$

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x - 3$. Then $fg(4) = f(1) = 2 \times 1 + 1 = 3$.

💡 Worked Example 2
With the same pair, $gf(4) = g(9) = 9 - 3 = 6$. Since $6 \ne 3$, the order of composition matters.

💡 Worked Example 3
$f(x) = 2x$ and $g(x) = x + 5$. Then $fg(x) = 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10$, while $gf(x) = 2x + 5$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
$fg(x)$ is not $f(x) \times g(x)$. It is one function applied after another, not a product.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Inside function first.
• $fg$ and $gf$ are usually different.

notes.heading: Inverse Functions: f⁻¹(x)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ undoes what $f$ does. If $f$ maps $a$ to $b$, then $f^{-1}$ maps $b$ back to $a$.

$$f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$

🔑 How it works
To invert $f(x) = ax + b$, reverse the operations in the reverse order: subtract $b$, then divide by $a$.

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = 3x + 6$. Undo: subtract 6, divide by 3, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 6}{3}$.

💡 Worked Example 2
Check with $x = 2$: $f(2) = 12$, and $f^{-1}(12) = \dfrac{12 - 6}{3} = 2$ — back where we started.

⚠️ Common Mistake
$f^{-1}(x)$ does not mean $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The $-1$ names the inverse; it is not a power or a reciprocal.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Undo in reverse order: the last operation done is the first one undone.
• Only one-to-one functions have inverse functions.

notes.heading: Chaining and Solving: ff(x) and Mixed Questions
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Exam questions chain these ideas: evaluate a composite, solve $f(a) = b$, or find $a$ from $ff(a)$ by applying the rule to itself, bracketed carefully.

💡 Worked Example 1
$f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $ff(a) = 43$. Then $f(f(a)) = 2(2a + 1) + 1 = 4a + 3$, so $4a + 3 = 43$, giving $a = 10$.

💡 Worked Example 2
$f(x) = 4x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$. Then $f(g(3)) = f(10) = 38$, but $g(f(3)) = g(10) = 101$. Same functions, different order, very different answers.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Expanding $2(2a + 1) + 1$ as $4a + 1$ — the outer '× 2' hits the whole bracket, and the outer '+ 1' still needs adding: $4a + 3$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always work in brackets, innermost first.
• Re-derive: plug your answer back through the chain to check it lands on the given output.

✅ Check
With $f(x) = 2x + 1$: $ff(1) = f(3) = 7$, which matches $4(1) + 3 = 7$.

questions.stem: Here is the function $f(x) = 4x - 1$. Work out $f(3)$.
questions.explanation: Substitute: $f(3) = 4 \times 3 - 1 = 11$. The option 12 comes from forgetting to subtract 1; 43 reverses the operations.

questions.stem: Here is the function $g(x) = x^2 + 2$. Work out $g(4)$.
questions.explanation: $g(4) = 4^2 + 2 = 16 + 2 = 18$. The option 16 forgets to add 2, and 20 squares the result instead of the input.

choices: The value of x when the output is 5
The number of outputs of the function
The output of the function when the input is 5
questions.explanation: f(5) is the output produced when 5 is fed into the rule of f. It is not f × 5, and the input 5 appears at the start of the mapping, not the end.

questions.stem: $h(x) = 3x$ and $h(a) = 21$. Work out the value of $a$.
questions.explanation: $3a = 21$, so $a = 21 \div 3 = 7$. The option 63 multiplies instead of dividing — a sign of mixing up which operation undoes 'times 3'.
The inverse undoes the original mapping, so $p^{-1}(9) = 2$: it returns the input that produced 9. The option 16 applies the rule again instead of undoing it.

questions.stem: $f(x) = 5x - 3$ and $f(a) = 27$. Work out the value of $a$.
questions.explanation: $5a - 3 = 27$, so $5a = 30$ and $a = 6$. Divide only after adding 3; 4.8 comes from $27 \div 5 - 3$-style scrambling of the order.

questions.stem: $f(x) = x^2$ with domain $\{-2, 0, 3\}$. Write down the range.
questions.explanation: Each input is squared: $(-2)^2 = 4$, $0^2 = 0$, $3^2 = 9$, so the range is $\{0, 4, 9\}$. Dropping 0 forgets the middle input.
Inside first: $g(4) = 1$, then $f(1) = 2 \times 1 + 1 = 3$. The option 6 is $gf(4)$, the composition in the wrong order.

questions.stem: Using $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x - 3$ from the previous question, work out $gf(4)$.
questions.explanation: $f(4) = 9$, then $g(9) = 9 - 3 = 6$. Notice $gf(4) = 6$ differs from $fg(4) = 3$: order of composition matters.
Undo 'times 3, add 6' in reverse: subtract 6, divide by 3, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 6}{3}$. Check: $f(2) = 12$ and $f^{-1}(12) = 2$.

questions.stem: $f(x) = 2x$ and $g(x) = x + 5$. Find an expression for $fg(x)$.
questions.explanation: $fg(x) = f(x + 5) = 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10$. The option $2x + 5$ is $gf(x)$, and $x + 10$ misplaces the doubling.
$g(3) = 3^2 + 1 = 10$, then $f(10) = 4 \times 10 - 2 = 38$. The option 101 is $g(f(3))$, the reverse order; 34 forgets the +1 inside $g$.
Undo 'times 3, subtract 5' in reverse: add 5, divide by 3, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 5}{3}$. Check with $x = 4$: $f(4) = 7$ and $f^{-1}(7) = 4$.

questions.stem: $f(x) = x^2 - 2$ on the integer domain $-3 \le x \le 2$. What is the smallest value in the range?
questions.explanation: The outputs are $7, 2, -1, -2, -1, 2$, so the smallest is $-2$, produced at $x = 0$. The largest |input| gives the biggest square, but the *smallest* output sits at the turning point.

questions.stem: $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $ff(a) = 43$. Work out the value of $a$.
questions.explanation: $f(f(a)) = 2(2a + 1) + 1 = 4a + 3$. Solve $4a + 3 = 43$: $a = 10$. The option 21 solves the rule only once; 10.5 comes from expanding wrongly as $4a + 1$.
